cards.title: Introduction to Spring Core & IoC Container
cards.content:
At the heart of the Spring Framework is the Inversion of Control (IoC) container. IoC is a design principle where the control of object creation and lifecycle management is transferred from the application code to a framework container.

The container is responsible for instantiating, configuring, and assembling objects known as Spring Beans.

ApplicationContext context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(AppConfig.class);
MyService service = context.getBean(MyService.class);

cards.title: IoC vs. Dependency Injection (DI)
cards.content:
While often used interchangeably, IoC and DI are distinct concepts:

  • Inversion of Control (IoC) is the broad principle (e.g., "Don't call us, we'll call you").
  • Dependency Injection (DI) is the specific pattern used to realize IoC, where dependencies are provided to an object rather than the object creating them itself.

options.text: ApplicationContext is a sub-interface of BeanFactory with advanced enterprise capabilities.
BeanFactory is a sub-interface of ApplicationContext.
ApplicationContext cannot load external configuration files.
BeanFactory is preferred over ApplicationContext for most standard web applications.

cards.title: The Spring Bean Lifecycle
cards.content:
A Spring Bean undergoes a well-defined lifecycle managed entirely by the IoC container. Key phases include:

  1. Instantiation: The bean instance is created in memory.
  2. Property Population: Dependencies are injected via setter or constructor injection.
  3. Initialization: Custom initialization methods (e.g., annotated with @PostConstruct) are invoked.
  4. Destruction: Bean resources are cleaned up before termination (e.g., annotated with @PreDestroy).

cards.title: Spring Configuration Styles
cards.content:
Spring allows you to configure your container using three main approaches:

  • Java-based Configuration: Uses classes annotated with @Configuration and methods annotated with @Bean.
  • Annotation-based Configuration: Uses stereotype annotations (like @Component) and automatic component scanning.
  • XML-based Configuration: Legacy approach defining beans in XML documents (discouraged in modern Spring Boot applications).

cards.title: Understanding Stereotype Annotations
cards.content:
Stereotype annotations are specialized forms of @Component that align with enterprise architecture layers:

  • @Controller: Handles web requests.
  • @Service: Encapsulates business logic.
  • @Repository: Interacts with the database and translates platform-specific exceptions into Spring DataAccessException.

cards.title: Types of Dependency Injection
cards.content:
Spring supports three main flavors of Dependency Injection:

  • Constructor Injection: Dependencies are passed via the constructor. Best practice as it allows for immutable beans and ensures required dependencies are not null.
  • Setter Injection: Dependencies are passed via setter methods. Useful for optional dependencies.
  • Field Injection: Injection directly into class fields using @Autowired. Discouraged as it hides dependencies and makes unit testing harder.

options.text: Field injection because it reduces boilerplate code lines.
Constructor injection because it promotes immutability and facilitates safe unit testing.
Setter injection because it is executed before any constructor calls.
XML injection because it keeps configuration decoupled from source code.

cards.title: Spring Core Best Practices
cards.content:
To build robust Spring applications, keep the following principles in mind:

  • Prefer Constructor Injection for mandatory dependencies.
  • Keep beans stateless by utilizing the default singleton scope carefully.
  • Avoid circular dependencies by refactoring code to separate responsibilities.
  • Utilize profile-based configurations (@Profile) to handle environment-specific configurations cleanly.
